The {{c1::word root}} is the foundation of a medical term — its main part or stem, carrying the core meaning.
Back Extra: Ex: in cardiology, cardi (heart) is the root.

Text: A {{c1::prefix}} is attached to the {{c2::beginning}} of a term and generally describes {{c3::location and intensity}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a suffix attaches to the END of the word.

Text: A {{c1::suffix}} is attached to the {{c2::end}} of a term and usually indicates a {{c3::procedure, condition, disease, or part of speech}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a prefix attaches to the BEGINNING of the word.

Text: A {{c1::combining vowel}} connects a word root to a suffix or to another word root, and is usually the vowel {{c2::o}} — sometimes i or e instead.
Back Extra: Ex: in gastroenterology, the two o's are combining vowels.

Text: A combining vowel is used between a word root and a suffix when the suffix begins with a {{c1::consonant}}, to make the term easier to pronounce.
Back Extra: Pitfall: drop the combining vowel when the suffix begins with a vowel (eg, gastr + -itis = gastritis).

Text: When a term has two word roots, a combining vowel is kept between them even when the second root {{c1::begins with a vowel}}.
Back Extra: Ex: gastr/o/enter/o/logy keeps the o between gastr and enter.

Text: Medical plural endings: singular {{c1::-a}} → -ae; {{c2::-is}} → -es; {{c3::-ex or -ix}} → -ices; {{c4::-on or -um}} → -a; {{c5::-us}} → -i.
Back Extra: Ex: vertebra→vertebrae; diagnosis→diagnoses; appendix→appendices; bacterium→bacteria; alveolus→alveoli.

Text: A patient sitting upright is placed in the {{c1::Fowler}} position.
Back Extra: Cue: think of raising the head of the bed or stretcher.

Text: The {{c1::semi-Fowler}} position reclines a patient to about {{c2::45°}}, while {{c1::high-Fowler}} sits them at about {{c2::90°}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the higher the Fowler name, the more upright the patient.
